questions.prompt: Which of these nouns does NOT form a fixed partnership with FIRST?
questions.explanation: English has first aid, the first time and a first impression — the very phrase this unit is named after — but never "first hatred". Feelings do not all behave alike: love comes at first sight, while hatred takes deep or bitter as its usual partners. Nothing in the meaning of the words explains the choice, so the only reliable test for a collocation is whether you have actually met it in real English.

questions.prompt: Match each British English word with the American English word that means the same.
questions.explanation: British luggage and American baggage both name the bags you travel with. The British walk on the pavement, Americans on the sidewalk. A British rubber and an American eraser both remove pencil marks. And the vehicle that carries goods is a lorry in Britain and a truck in the United States. Neither column is more correct than the other — they are two varieties of one language — but a text has to stay inside the variety it started in, so a British lorry never parks in an American paragraph.

questions.prompt: "After many disagreements, the two families decided to put aside their differences." Here, to put aside means to…
questions.explanation: Put aside carries several meanings, and the words that follow it decide which one applies: with money it means to save (put aside money for a rainy day), with a newspaper it means to lay something down for a moment, and with differences, fears or doubts it means to forget them, to disregard them, to leave them behind. Reading it as saving something for later takes the money sense into a sentence that does not fit it. This is why a dictionary of synonyms lists a phrasal verb example by example instead of once and for all — and why you read the whole sentence before you choose a meaning.

questions.prompt: This line comes from the last pages of a school book: "Bouzid, S. 2014. Reading Skills for Secondary Classes. Tunis: Nour Publishing." What kind of text is it, and what does 2014 stand for?

options.text: a bibliography — the date of publication
a bibliography — the number of pages
a receipt — the date of the purchase
an advertisement — the price of the book in dinars

questions.explanation: A line built as last name, initial of the first name, year, title of the book, then place and publisher is an entry in a bibliography, and the four-figure number placed just after the initial is always the date of publication — 2014 here. Nothing in the line counts pages, records a purchase or names a price: a receipt would show an amount paid and the shop's exchange policy, and an advertisement would praise the book instead of identifying it. A bibliography identifies; it never sells.

questions.prompt: Complete: "My aunt bought some ___ to bake a cake for my sister's wedding." Which spelling is right?
questions.explanation: Flour is the powder made from wheat, and it is what a cake is made of; flower is the part of a plant that opens in spring, and a wedding cake is only decorated with those. The two words sound exactly the same, which makes them homophones, so nothing but the sentence around them can tell you which one to write — and no spellchecker will ever catch the mistake, because both words exist. Floor and flow look close on the page but sound different and mean something else again.

questions.prompt: Sonia grew up speaking Arabic with her family and French at school. Which word describes her?
questions.explanation: The prefix bi- means two, so a speaker of two languages is bilingual. Mono- means one, and a monolingual speaker has only one language; multi- means many, so multilingual describes somebody who handles several. The same prefixes are at work on the word culture — bicultural, multicultural — which is why reading the prefix is very often enough to read the whole word.
